questions.question: Define mechanical advantage as a ratio, and explain what values greater than 1, equal to 1 and less than 1 tell you about a machine, with an example of each.
questions.expected_answer: Mechanical advantage is load divided by effort. Greater than 1: the machine multiplies force and makes the user stronger, for example a car jack or a crowbar. Equal to 1: the machine changes only the direction or position of the force, for example a single fixed pulley or a seesaw with equal arms. Less than 1: the user must push harder than the load but the load moves faster or further, for example a bicycle in top gear or a fishing rod. The price of a mechanical advantage above 1 is always a greater distance moved by the effort.

questions.question: Name the six simple machines and give one everyday example of each.
questions.expected_answer: Lever (crowbar, seesaw, scissors); wheel and axle (doorknob, steering wheel, bicycle pedals); pulley (flagpole rope, crane hoist); inclined plane (ramp, plank for loading a drum); wedge (axe, knife blade, door wedge); screw (vice, bottle cap, wood screw).

questions.question: Explain what is meant by a complex machine and identify at least four simple machines inside a bicycle, naming the part each one corresponds to.
questions.expected_answer: A complex machine is a combination of simple machines in which the output of one becomes the input of the next. In a bicycle: pedals and crank arms are a wheel and axle; chain and sprockets are gears; brake levers are levers; handlebars turning the fork are a wheel and axle; the saddle clamp or quick-release is a screw; the rear wheel on its axle is another wheel and axle.
